question: Between 22 June and 20 October 2026, where did the radar signal over the Ciénaga Grande change — and does comparing HH with HV tell us whether the change happened at the surface or in the vegetation above it?
collection: PROVISIONAL (CRID P05023), the same for both dates
lead_conclusion: The water surface changed — the lagoon did not grow.
measured_over_open_water: HH echo rose by about +3 dB; HV rose only about +0.5 dB; over land HH did not move
wind_check: wind at the overpass hour was 3.4 times weaker on the brighter date, so a windier surface does not explain it
processing: boxcar 5×5 px speckle filter; change = 10·log10(after/before) in dB
why_it_changed: What we measured Open water: 329 → 344 km² (+4%). The lagoon's size barely changed. Over open water, the HH echo rose by about +3 dB ; over land it did not move. Over the same water, HV rose only about +0.5 dB . Wind at the overpass hour was 3.4× weaker on the brighter date (NASA POWER), so a windier surface does not explain it. Why this points to the surface NISAR's L-band radar sends its own pulse and records the echo. Calm open water reflects the pulse away and looks dark; a rougher or shallower surface sends more of it back. HH responds strongly to the surface itself, while HV rises when the pulse scatters inside vegetation. HH up with HV almost flat points to a change at the water surface, not to new plants above it (NASA Earthdata, n.d.; Jensen et al., 2018). Open hypotheses — to test, not claimed A local breeze that the coarse wind model (0.5° cell) cannot resolve. Rain falling on the water at the overpass time. Very shallow water or emergent features near the shore. Floating vegetation is less likely: it would also raise HV. What we do not claim Two dates cannot show a trend or prove a cause. We do not claim damage, long-term change or predictions. Next check: rainfall for both dates (NASA GPM IMERG). Sources: NASA Earthdata (n.d.), Synthetic Aperture Radar ; Jensen et al. (2018), Remote Sensing 10(9):1431; NASA POWER WS10M at the acquisition hours.

change_types_ai.method: k-means (unsupervised AI) groups of how HH and HV changed together, named by fixed rules; the names are interpretations, not ground truth

radar: NISAR sends its own L-band pulse, about 24 cm long, and records the echo, so it sees day and night, through cloud and smoke. It revisits every 12 days.
how_to_read: Calm water reflects the pulse away and looks dark; rough ground, tree crowns and broken ice scatter it back and look bright. A change in the echo is a change in roughness or moisture; floods, harvest or ice movement are interpretations of it.
collections: NISAR data come in successive collections (BETA, PROVISIONAL, VALIDATED). The app only compares two dates inside one collection and CRID.
